item.title: Elbow — Myofascial Release
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Elbow and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: elbow flexion/extension, forearm rotation, grip and load-related pain.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Sitting or supine with the upper limb supported.
Keep wrist and shoulder relaxed unless movement is part of the technique.
therapistPosition: Stand or sit beside the arm with the elbow supported close to the body.
stabilization: Stabilize humerus or forearm according to the target joint/tissue.
contact: Use broad contact around the ulnohumeral/radiocapitellar region or target soft tissue; protect the ulnar nerve and radial head region.
Use broad skin/fascial contact over the relevant soft-tissue region with enough grip to engage tissue without slipping.
Direct work follows the perceived restriction; indirect work follows the direction of ease.
forceDirection: Apply slow sustained multidirectional loading rather than a fast thrust.
Pressure is adjusted to comfort, tissue response and the intended direct/indirect strategy.
dosage: Sustained contacts are commonly held 60–120 seconds or until a clear change is felt, with reassessment rather than fixed over-treatment.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Elbow: elbow flexion/extension, forearm rotation, grip and load-related pain.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid aggressive treatment with suspected fracture, unstable ligament injury, acute nerve irritation or major swelling.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Elbow assessment → correct regional setup → Myofascial Release → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Forearm Extensor Fascial Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve forearm soft-tissue tolerance before grip and progressive loading.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Sitting with forearm supported and wrist relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Broad hand/thumb/forearm contact along extensor muscle bellies rather than directly on the lateral epicondyle.
subTechniques.direction: Apply slow longitudinal or oblique fascial load; wrist movement may be added gently if comfortable.
subTechniques.reassess: Grip, wrist motion and local forearm pain.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Avoid spending the whole session on manual work—follow with graded extensor loading.
